title: Differential Entropy: Gibbs Inequality and Gaussian Maximum Entropy
description: Formalizes differential entropy h(f) = -∫ f(x)ln f(x)dx for continuous distributions using Mathlib's Bochner integral. Proves the continuous Gibbs inequality, translation invariance, scale equivariance, Gaussian entropy, and the Gaussian maximum entropy theorem.

meta.author: Lean Genius
meta.assumptions: None. Fully machine-verified from Mathlib. Uses Bochner integral and Gaussian integration.
originalContributions: kl_divergence_continuous_nonneg: D(f||g) ≥ 0 (continuous KL divergence is non-negative)
gibbs_inequality_continuous: h(f) ≤ -∫ f·ln g for any reference density g
differentialEntropy_scale_equivariant: h(g) = h(f) + ln|a| when g(x) = (1/|a|)f(x/a)
gaussian_max_entropy: among densities with variance ≤ σ², the Gaussian maximizes differential entropy

overview.historicalContext:
Differential entropy h(X) = -∫ f(x)ln f(x)dx was introduced by Shannon (1948) as the continuous analogue of discrete entropy H(X) = -∑ p(x)log p(x). Unlike discrete entropy, differential entropy can be negative (e.g., Uniform[0,a] has h = ln a < 0 for a < 1) and is not truly a measure of information in the same sense.

The Gaussian maximum entropy theorem — that among all distributions with a given variance, the Gaussian has the highest differential entropy — is a cornerstone of information theory. It underpins maximum entropy inference, channel capacity results, and statistical mechanics.

This formalization answers the OQ from the Shannon Entropy gallery: 'Can differential entropy h(X) = -∫ f(x)ln f(x)dx be formalized in Lean using Mathlib's measure theory?' Answer: YES, using Mathlib's Bochner integral.
overview.problemStatement: Formalize differential entropy for continuous distributions using Lean/Mathlib's measure theory, including: (1) the continuous Gibbs inequality D(f||g) ≥ 0, (2) translation and scale invariance, (3) Gaussian entropy h(N(μ,σ²)) = ½ ln(2πeσ²), and (4) the Gaussian maximum entropy theorem.
overview.proofStrategy:
**KL divergence / Gibbs inequality**: Uses the real-analysis inequality t - 1 ≥ ln t (equivalently, ln(f/g) ≤ f/g - 1) applied to the ratio f/g pointwise, then integrates.

**Translation invariance**: Lebesgue measure is translation-invariant, so ∫ f(x-c)·ln(f(x-c)) dx = ∫ f(y)·ln(f(y)) dy by `integral_add_right_eq_self`.

**Scale equivariance**: Change of variables x → x/a using `Measure.integral_comp_div`.

**Gaussian entropy**: Compute directly using the explicit Gaussian PDF, its normalization, second moment ∫ x²·N(μ,σ²)dx = σ², and the log structure of the Gaussian.

**Maximum entropy**: Apply the Gibbs inequality with g = Gaussian: h(f) ≤ -∫ f·ln(Gaussian) = ½ ln(2πeσ²).
keyInsights: Real.log 0 = 0 in Mathlib makes the 0·ln(0) = 0 convention automatic — no special casing needed
The continuous Gibbs inequality reduces to the pointwise inequality ln(p/q) ≤ p/q - 1 (analogous to lnx ≤ x-1)
Translation invariance uses integral_add_right_eq_self from Mathlib (Lebesgue measure is shift-invariant)
Gaussian second moment ∫ x²·exp(-bx²) dx = ½√(π/b³) is proved via integration by parts using G(x)=-x/(2b)·exp(-bx²)
The maximum entropy proof is elegant: apply Gibbs with the Gaussian as reference density

Scale equivariance uses Measure.integral_comp_div — the change-of-variables theorem for Lebesgue integrals under linear maps — which gives ∫ f(x/a) dx = |a|·∫ f(x) dx, yielding h(g) = h(f) + ln|a| after log-splitting
prerequisites: Real.log convexity and the inequality ln(t) ≤ t-1
integral_gaussian: ∫ exp(-bx²) dx = √(π/b) (Gaussian integral in Mathlib)
Measure.integral_comp_div: change of variables by division

sections.title: Definitions
sections.mathContext: Differential entropy is defined via the Bochner integral: `differentialEntropy f = -∫ x, f x * Real.log (f x)`. The sign convention comes from writing $h(f) = -\int f(x) \ln f(x) \,dx$ where $f(x) \ln f(x) < 0$ when $f(x) \in (0,1)$, so the negation gives a positive contribution for spread-out densities. Critically, `Real.log 0 = 0` in Mathlib makes the convention $0 \cdot \ln 0 = 0$ automatic — no special case is needed. The KL divergence (relative entropy) `klDivergenceCts f g = ∫ x, f x * Real.log (f x / g x)` measures the "information gain" of using $f$ instead of $g$; it equals $h_{\mathrm{cross}}(f,g) - h(f)$ where $h_{\mathrm{cross}}$ is cross-entropy. The Bochner integral returns 0 when the function is non-integrable, making both definitions total (well-defined for any $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$); theorems require integrability hypotheses.

sections.title: Gibbs Inequality
sections.summary: kl_divergence_continuous_nonneg: D(f||g) ≥ 0. gibbs_inequality_continuous: h(f) ≤ -∫ f·ln g.
sections.mathContext: The continuous Gibbs inequality is proved via a pointwise reduction to the analytic inequality $\ln t \leq t - 1$ for $t > 0$. The private lemma `kl_term_bound_cts` proves $p \cdot \ln(p/q) \geq p - q$ for $p, q > 0$: from $\ln(q/p) \leq q/p - 1$ (which is $\ln t \leq t-1$ at $t = q/p$), multiply both sides by $p$ and negate. `kl_divergence_continuous_nonneg` integrates this bound: $\int f \ln(f/g) \geq \int (f - g) = 1 - 1 = 0$, using the probability measure conditions $\int f = 1$ and $\int g = 1$. The Gibbs inequality `gibbs_inequality_continuous` then follows: $h(f) = -\int f \ln f = \int f \ln(1/f) = \int f \ln(g/f) + \int f \ln(1/g) \leq 0 + (-\int f \ln g)$, since $\int f \ln(g/f) = -D(f \| g) \leq 0$. This is the fundamental inequality of information theory: the entropy of $f$ is bounded above by the cross-entropy with any reference density $g$.

sections.title: Translation and Scale Invariance
sections.summary: differentialEntropy_translation_invariant: h(f(·-c)) = h(f). differentialEntropy_scale_equivariant: h((1/|a|)f(·/a)) = h(f) + ln|a|.
sections.mathContext: Two symmetry results characterize differential entropy under affine transformations. **Translation invariance** (`differentialEntropy_translation_invariant`): $h(f(\cdot - c)) = h(f)$. The proof uses `integral_add_right_eq_self` from Mathlib, which implements the Lebesgue measure invariance $\int g(x - c) \,dx = \int g(x) \,dx$; applying this with $g(x) = f(x) \cdot \ln f(x)$ gives the result immediately. **Scale equivariance** (`differentialEntropy_scale_equivariant`): if $g(x) = (1/|a|) f(x/a)$, then $h(g) = h(f) + \ln|a|$. The proof uses `Measure.integral_comp_div` (change of variables $x \to x/a$): $\int g(x) \ln g(x) \,dx = \frac{1}{|a|} \int f(y)(\ln f(y) - \ln|a|) \,dy = \int f \ln f - \ln|a|$, giving $h(g) = h(f) + \ln|a|$. The factor $+\ln|a|$ reflects that expanding the support by $|a|$ increases uncertainty; for $|a| < 1$ the entropy decreases, consistent with differential entropy being negative for concentrated distributions.

sections.title: Gaussian Entropy
sections.summary: gaussianDifferentialEntropy: h(N(μ,σ²)) = ½ ln(2πeσ²). Proved using Gaussian PDF, normalization, and second moment.
sections.mathContext: The Gaussian PDF is `gaussianPDF μ σ x = (1/(σ * Real.sqrt (2*π))) * Real.exp (-(x-μ)^2 / (2*σ^2))`. The entropy computation `gaussianDifferentialEntropy` evaluates $h(\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)) = \tfrac{1}{2} \ln(2\pi e \sigma^2)$ by splitting the log: $\ln(\text{gaussianPDF}(x)) = -\tfrac{1}{2}\ln(2\pi\sigma^2) - \tfrac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}$. Integrating against $f = \text{gaussianPDF}$ gives two terms: (1) $-\int f \cdot (-\tfrac{1}{2}\ln(2\pi\sigma^2)) \,dx = \tfrac{1}{2}\ln(2\pi\sigma^2)$ (by Gaussian normalization $\int f = 1$); (2) $-\int f \cdot (-(x-\mu)^2/(2\sigma^2)) \,dx = \mathbb{E}[(X-\mu)^2]/(2\sigma^2) = \sigma^2/(2\sigma^2) = \tfrac{1}{2}$ (using the second moment). Combining: $h = \tfrac{1}{2}\ln(2\pi\sigma^2) + \tfrac{1}{2} = \tfrac{1}{2}\ln(2\pi e \sigma^2)$. The second moment computation requires integrating $x^2 e^{-bx^2}$, handled via integration by parts with antiderivative $G(x) = -x/(2b) \cdot e^{-bx^2}$.

sections.title: Gaussian Maximum Entropy Theorem
sections.summary: gaussian_max_entropy: among densities with ∫ x²f ≤ σ², h(f) ≤ ½ ln(2πeσ²). Proved via Gibbs inequality with Gaussian reference.
sections.mathContext: `gaussian_max_entropy` proves that the Gaussian uniquely maximizes differential entropy among all distributions with second moment $\leq \sigma^2$: if $f$ is a probability density with $\int x^2 f(x) \,dx \leq \sigma^2$, then $h(f) \leq \tfrac{1}{2}\ln(2\pi e \sigma^2)$. The proof is a one-line application of the Gibbs inequality with reference density $g = \text{gaussianPDF}(0, \sigma)$: $h(f) \leq -\int f \ln g = \int f \left[\tfrac{x^2}{2\sigma^2} + \tfrac{1}{2}\ln(2\pi\sigma^2)\right] \,dx = \tfrac{1}{2\sigma^2} \int x^2 f + \tfrac{1}{2}\ln(2\pi\sigma^2) \leq \tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{1}{2}\ln(2\pi\sigma^2) = \tfrac{1}{2}\ln(2\pi e\sigma^2)$. This is the formal version of the maximum entropy principle, which underlies the Gaussian noise model in information theory: the worst-case noise (maximizing channel uncertainty) under a power constraint is Gaussian.

conclusion.summary: Formalizes differential entropy for continuous distributions: continuous Gibbs inequality, translation and scale invariance, Gaussian entropy h(N(μ,σ²)) = ½ ln(2πeσ²), and Gaussian maximum entropy theorem. 623 lines, 6 public theorems, 3 definitions, 0 sorries, 0 axioms.
conclusion.implications: This formalization confirms that Mathlib's Bochner integral is sufficient to handle differential entropy rigorously. The 0·ln(0) = 0 convention is automatic. The Gaussian maximum entropy theorem gives a formal foundation for maximum entropy methods in Bayesian inference and statistical physics.
